claim: During the initial stages of axon outgrowth, microtubules display mixed polarity in Drosophila neurons.
source: We showed that, during the initial stages of axon outgrowth, microtubules display mixed polarity and minus-end-out microtubules push the tip of the axon, consistent with kinesin-1 driving outgrowth by sliding antiparallel microtubules.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the results section showing EB1 comet tracking in developing neurons.

claim: Minus-end-out microtubules push the tip of the axon during initial stages of axon outgrowth.
source: We showed that, during the initial stages of axon outgrowth, microtubules display mixed polarity and minus-end-out microtubules push the tip of the axon, consistent with kinesin-1 driving outgrowth by sliding antiparallel microtubules.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by CAMSAP3 localization data showing minus-ends at growing neurite tips.

claim: Kinesin-1 drives axon outgrowth by sliding antiparallel microtubules.
source: We showed that, during the initial stages of axon outgrowth, microtubules display mixed polarity and minus-end-out microtubules push the tip of the axon, consistent with kinesin-1 driving outgrowth by sliding antiparallel microtubules.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the abstract and is consistent with the observed mixed polarity and minus-end-out orientation data.

claim: At later stages of development, microtubule orientation in the axon switches from mixed to uniform polarity with plus-end-out.
source: At later stages, the microtubule orientation in the axon switches from mixed to uniform polarity with plus-end-out.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by EB1 comet tracking data at different time points showing the transition from mixed to uniform polarity.

claim: Dynein knockdown prevents microtubule rearrangement from mixed to uniform polarity in axons.
source: Dynein knockdown prevents this rearrangement and results in microtubules of mixed orientation in axons and accumulation of microtubule minus-ends at axon tips.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing EB1 comet directionality in dynein RNAi neurons.

claim: Dynein knockdown results in accumulation of microtubule minus-ends at axon tips.
source: Dynein knockdown prevents this rearrangement and results in microtubules of mixed orientation in axons and accumulation of microtubule minus-ends at axon tips.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by CAMSAP3 localization data in dynein RNAi conditions.

claim: Microtubule reorganization requires recruitment of dynein to the actin cortex.
source: Microtubule reorganization requires recruitment of dynein to the actin cortex, as actin depolymerization phenocopies dynein depletion, and direct recruitment of dynein to the membrane bypasses the actin requirement.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by LatB treatment experiments and dynein membrane recruitment experiments.

claim: Actin depolymerization phenocopies dynein depletion in terms of microtubule organization.
source: Microtubule reorganization requires recruitment of dynein to the actin cortex, as actin depolymerization phenocopies dynein depletion, and direct recruitment of dynein to the membrane bypasses the actin requirement.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing similar microtubule orientation defects after LatB treatment and dynein knockdown.

claim: Direct recruitment of dynein to the membrane bypasses the actin requirement for microtubule sorting.
source: Microtubule reorganization requires recruitment of dynein to the actin cortex, as actin depolymerization phenocopies dynein depletion, and direct recruitment of dynein to the membrane bypasses the actin requirement.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by rapalog-induced BicD-dynein recruitment experiments showing microtubule sorting in the absence of F-actin.

claim: Cortical dynein slides minus-end-out microtubules from the axon, generating uniform microtubule arrays.
source: Our results show that cortical dynein slides 'minus-end-out' microtubules from the axon, generating uniform microtubule arrays.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by LatB washout experiments showing retrograde movement of CAMSAP3-labeled minus-ends.

claim: Differences in microtubule orientation between axons and dendrites could be dictated by differential activity of cortical dynein.
source: We speculate that differences in microtubule orientation between axons and dendrites could be dictated by differential activity of cortical dynein.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation in the abstract.

claim: Kinesin-1 slides microtubules against each other in many cell types including neurons.
source: Recently, our lab demonstrated that kinesin-1, a major microtubule motor, slides microtubules against each other in many cell types (Jolly et al., 2010; Barlan et al., 2013), including neurons, and this sliding plays an important role in neuronal polarization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: Microtubule-microtubule sliding is required for initial axon formation and regeneration after injury.
source: We have shown that microtubule-microtubule sliding is required for initial axon formation and regeneration after injury (Lu et al., 2013b; 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Kinesin-driven microtubule sliding has been implicated in generating the minus-end-out microtubule pattern observed in dendrites of Caenorhabditis elegans neurons.
source: This process is likely required for neurodevelopment in many organisms besides Drosophila, as kinesin-driven microtubule sliding has been implicated in generating the minus-end-out microtubule pattern observed in dendrites of Caenorhabditis elegans neurons (Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to published work.

claim: Kinesin-1 is a heterotetramer that consists of two heavy chains (KHC) and two light chains.
source: Each kinesin-1 molecule is a heterotetramer that consists of two heavy chains (KHC) and two light chains (Kuznetsov et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Each KHC polypeptide contains two microtubule-binding domains: one ATP-dependent site in the motor domain and a second ATP-independent site at the C-terminus.
source: Each KHC polypeptide contains two microtubule-binding domains: one ATP-dependent site in the motor domain and a second ATP-independent site at the C-terminus (Hackney and Stock, 2000; Seeger and Rice, 2010; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Kinesin-1 slides microtubules against each other using its two heavy chain domains; one microtubule is used as a track, while the other is transported as a cargo.
source: Kinesin-1 is thought to slide microtubules against each other with these two heavy chain domains; one microtubule is used as a track, while the other is transported as a cargo; kinesin light chains are not required for sliding (Jolly et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This mechanism is stated with citations to supporting work.

claim: Kinesin light chains are not required for microtubule sliding.
source: Kinesin-1 is thought to slide microtubules against each other with these two heavy chain domains; one microtubule is used as a track, while the other is transported as a cargo; kinesin light chains are not required for sliding (Jolly et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting work.

claim: Axons contain microtubule arrays of uniform orientation with plus-ends facing the axon tip.
source: Axons contain microtubule arrays of uniform orientation with plus-ends facing the axon tip (Baas et al., 1988; Stone et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Kinesin-1 is a plus-end motor and can only slide microtubules with their minus-ends leading and plus-ends trailing.
source: However, kinesin-1 is a plus-end motor, and therefore can only slide microtubules with their minus-ends leading and plus-ends trailing (Figure 1A), which is inconsistent with the final orientation of microtubules in mature axons.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of kinesin-1's motor properties and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Bidirectional microtubule movement can be observed in growing axons of cultured Drosophila neurons using tubulin tagged with a photoconvertible probe.
source: Bidirectional microtubule movement can indeed be observed in growing axons of cultured Drosophila neurons using tubulin tagged with a photoconvertible probe (Video 1).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Video 1 showing the experimental observation.

claim: S2 cells can be induced to form cellular processes when the integrity of the actin filament network is impaired by treatment with either Cytochalasin D or Latrunculin B.
source: S2 cells provide a good model system to explore the mechanism of process formation because they canbe induced to form cellular processes when the integrity of the actin filament network is impaired by treatment with either Cytochalasin D or Latrunculin B (LatB) (Kim et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: CAMSAP proteins bind to microtubule minus-ends and stabilize them against depolymerization.
source: CAMSAP proteins bind to microtubule minus-ends and stabilize them against depolymerization, making them the perfect candidate to label microtubule minus-ends (Akhmanova and Hoogenraad, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Mammalian CAMSAP3 tagged with GFP expressed at consistently higher levels than Drosophila Patronin in S2 cells and reliably decorated microtubule ends.
source: On the other hand, its mammalian ortholog CAMSAP3 tagged with GFP expressed at consistently higher levels and reliably decorated microtubule ends (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only one end of each microtubule fragment contains a GFP-CAMSAP3 patch after partial depolymerization with Vinblastine.
source: Examination of these short microtubule fragments demonstrated that only one end of each microtubule contained a GFP-CAMSAP3 patch (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Spontaneous growth and shrinkage events associated with dynamic instability of microtubule plus-ends were not seen in microtubule ends decorated by GFP-CAMSAP3 in untreated S2 cells.
source: In untreated S2 cells, spontaneous growth and shrinkage events associated with the dynamic instability of microtubule plus-ends were not seen in microtubule ends decorated by GFP-CAMSAP3, suggesting that GFP-CAMSAP3 labels microtubule minus-ends in Drosophila cells (Video 2).
evidence: This observation is stated with reference to Video 2.

claim: EB1-GFP and mCherry-CAMSAP3 never colocalized when expressed in the same S2 cell.
source: Furthermore, EB1-GFP and mCherry-CAMSAP3 never colocalized when expressed in the same cell, further confirming the minus-end localization of CAMSAP3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C; Video 3).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C and Video 3.

claim: Mammalian GFP-CAMSAP3 reliably marks microtubule minus-ends in Drosophila.
source: These results, together with published data (Tanaka et al., 2012; Hendershott and Vale, 2014; Jiang et al., 2014; Akhmanova and Hoogenraad, 2015), demonstrated that mammalian GFP-CAMSAP3 reliably marks microtubule minus-ends in Drosophila.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the authors' data and published literature.

claim: A significant fraction of growing processes in S2 cells contained GFP-CAMSAP3 dots at their tips.
source: We found that a significant fraction of growing processes contained GFP-CAMSAP3 dots at their tips, and that these processes only elongated when microtubule minus-ends were present at their tips (Figure 1C,D; Video 4).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1C,D and Video 4.

claim: S2 cell processes only elongated when microtubule minus-ends were present at their tips.
source: We found that a significant fraction of growing processes contained GFP-CAMSAP3 dots at their tips, and that these processes only elongated when microtubule minus-ends were present at their tips (Figure 1C,D; Video 4).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1C,D and Video 4.

claim: Retraction of the GFP-CAMSAP3 marker from the process tip always coincided with a pause in process outgrowth in S2 cells.
source: Interestingly, we often observed retraction of the GFP-CAMSAP3 marker from the process tip; these events always coincided with a pause in process outgrowth (Figure 1C, inset).
evidence: This observation is stated with reference to Figure 1C inset.

claim: CAMSAP3 almost always colocalized with the tips of growing processes in S2 cells, while EB1 could only be found in the tips approximately 30% of the time.
source: Quantitative analysis demonstrated that while CAMSAP3 almost always colocalized with the tips of the growing processes, the plus-ends marker EB1 could only be found in the tips of the growing processes approximately 30% of the time (Figure 1E,F), suggesting that at this stage microtubule dynamics does not play a major role in process outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: At the initial stages of process outgrowth in S2 cells, microtubule dynamics does not play a major role in process outgrowth.
source: Quantitative analysis demonstrated that while CAMSAP3 almost always colocalized with the tips of the growing processes, the plus-ends marker EB1 could only be found in the tips of the growing processes approximately 30% of the time (Figure 1E,F), suggesting that at this stage microtubule dynamics does not play a major role in process outgrowth.
evidence: This interpretation is stated based on the quantitative analysis of CAMSAP3 and EB1 localization.

claim: Growing neurites in 4 hr cultured Drosophila neurons contained GFP-CAMSAP3 dots at the tips of neurites.
source: We found that, like in S2 cells, the growing neurites contained GFP-CAMSAP3 dots at the tips of neurites, and localization of the dots to the tips precisely correlated with neurite outgrowth (Figure 1G–I; Video 5).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1G–I and Video 5.

claim: Localization of GFP-CAMSAP3 dots to neurite tips precisely correlated with neurite outgrowth in Drosophila neurons.
source: We found that, like in S2 cells, the growing neurites contained GFP-CAMSAP3 dots at the tips of neurites, and localization of the dots to the tips precisely correlated with neurite outgrowth (Figure 1G–I; Video 5).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1G–I and Video 5.

claim: At least a fraction of microtubules in growing neurites have minus-end-out orientation.
source: All together, these data show that at least a fraction of microtubules in growing neurites have the 'wrong' orientation (minus-end-out).
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the CAMSAP3 localization data.

claim: Localization of microtubule minus-end(s) at the neurite tip correlates with neurite outgrowth.
source: Localization of microtubule minus-end(s) at the neurite tip correlates with neurite outgrowth, consistent with kinesin-1 pushing the minus-ends of microtubules against the plasma membrane driving the initial outgrowth.
evidence: This correlation is stated based on the experimental observations.

claim: Shortly after plating, growing neurites in cultured Drosophila neurons contained EB1 comets moving in both anterograde and retrograde directions.
source: Quantitative analysis of EB1-GFP comets using tracking software (see Material and methods) demonstrated that, shortly after plating, growing neurites contained EB1 comets moving in both anterograde and retrograde directions (Figure 2A,B; Video 6).
evidence: This is stated based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2A,B and Video 6.

claim: Microtubule orientation in axons remained mixed during the 1st day in culture.
source: The microtubule orientation in axons remained mixed during the 1st day in culture.
evidence: This is stated based on EB1 comet tracking data at different time points.

claim: At 36 hr in culture, the fraction of retrograde EB1 comets in axons started to decline.
source: At 36 hr, the fraction of retrograde EB1 comets started to decline, and at 48 hr, developed axons were mostly filled with plus-end-out microtubules (Figure 2A,B; Video 6).
evidence: This is stated based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2A,B and Video 6.

claim: At 48 hr in culture, developed axons were mostly filled with plus-end-out microtubules.
source: At 36 hr, the fraction of retrograde EB1 comets started to decline, and at 48 hr, developed axons were mostly filled with plus-end-out microtubules (Figure 2A,B; Video 6).
evidence: This is stated based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2A,B and Video 6.

claim: Axons initially contain microtubule arrays with mixed orientation.
source: These results demonstrated that axons initially contain microtubule arrays with mixed orientation.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the EB1 comet tracking data.

claim: Mutations in dynein light intermediate chain or dynein-cofactors (NudE) are required for uniform microtubule orientation in axons of Drosophila dendritic arborization (da) neurons.
source: We hypothesized that this sorting factor is cytoplasmic dynein because it has been reported that mutations in dynein light intermediate chain or dynein-cofactors (NudE) are required for uniform microtubule orientation in axons of Drosophila dendritic arborization (da) neurons (Zheng et al., 2008; Arthur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: elav>DHC RNAi animals developed to the third instar larval stage but their locomotion was severely impaired.
source: elav>DHC RNAi animals developed to the third instar larval stage; however, their locomotion was severely impaired and most died before reaching the pupae stage (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: Most elav>DHC RNAi animals died before reaching the pupae stage.
source: elav>DHC RNAi animals developed to the third instar larval stage; however, their locomotion was severely impaired and most died before reaching the pupae stage (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: None of the surviving elav>DHC RNAi pupae eclosed into adults.
source: In addition, none of the surviving elav>DHC RNAi pupae eclosed into adults.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: Mitochondrial movement was substantially diminished in elav>DHC RNAi neurons.
source: Our lab has previously shown that mitochondrial movement was substantially diminished in elav>DHC RNAi neurons, indicating that the activity of dynein is impaired in those neurons (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Analysis of EB1 comets in elav>DHC RNAi 48 hr-neurons revealed that axons contained microtubule arrays of mixed orientation.
source: Analysis of EB1 comets in elav>DHC RNAi 48 hr-neurons revealed that axons contained microtubule arrays of mixed orientation (Figure 2C,D; Video 7), suggesting that dynein is necessary to remove minus-end-out microtubules from axons.
evidence: This is stated based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C,D and Video 7.

claim: Dynein is necessary to remove minus-end-out microtubules from axons.
source: Analysis of EB1 comets in elav>DHC RNAi 48 hr-neurons revealed that axons contained microtubule arrays of mixed orientation (Figure 2C,D; Video 7), suggesting that dynein is necessary to remove minus-end-out microtubules from axons.
evidence: This interpretation is stated based on the dynein RNAi phenotype.

claim: Microtubule minus-ends in control neurons were scattered throughout the length of the axons.
source: Interestingly, while microtubule minus-ends in control neurons, as visualized by GFP-CAMSAP3, were scattered throughout the length of the axons, inactivation of dynein resulted in dramatic accumulation of the minus-end markers at neurite tips (Figure 2E; control, left panels; DHC-RNAi, right panels).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Inactivation of dynein resulted in dramatic accumulation of minus-end markers at neurite tips in neurons.
source: Interestingly, while microtubule minus-ends in control neurons, as visualized by GFP-CAMSAP3, were scattered throughout the length of the axons, inactivation of dynein resulted in dramatic accumulation of the minus-end markers at neurite tips (Figure 2E; control, left panels; DHC-RNAi, right panels).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Treatment of S2 cells with DHC dsRNA efficiently knocked down DHC.
source: The treatment of S2 cells with DHC dsRNA efficiently knocked down DHC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated based on Western blot and functional assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Dynein depletion in S2 cells resulted in processes with EB1-GFP comets traveling in both directions.
source: Recapitulating the neuronal phenotype, dynein depletion in S2 cells resulted in processes with EB1-GFP comets traveling in both directions (Figure 2F,G; Video 8).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2F,G and Video 8.

claim: In control S2 cells, GFP-CAMSAP3 has a broad, scattered dot distribution.
source: In control cells, GFP-CAMSAP3 has a broad, scattered dot distribution (Figure 2H, left panel).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Dynein depletion induced a striking en masse accumulation of CAMSAP3 at the tips of S2 cell processes.
source: Dynein depletion induced a striking en masse accumulation of CAMSAP3 at the tips of processes (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2H,I.

claim: Identical phenotypes (mixed polarity of GFP-EB1 comets and accumulation of CAMSAP3 at the tips of the processes) were observed after knocking down several dynein cofactors (p150Glued, Lis1 or NudE) in S2 cells.
source: Identical phenotypes (mixed polarity of GFP-EB1 comets and accumulation of CAMSAP3 at the tips of the processes) were observed after knocking down several dynein cofactors (p150Glued, Lis1 or NudE; Figure 2G–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B for knockdown efficiency).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The en masse accumulation of microtubule minus-ends at neurite tips and S2 processes in dynein RNAi cells is consistent with the idea that while kinesin-driven sliding stays intact, the sorting mechanism is inactivated by dynein depletion.
source: The en masse accumulation of microtubule minus-ends at neurite tips and S2 processes in dynein RNAi cells is consistent with the idea while kinesin-driven sliding stays intact, the sorting mechanism is inactivated by dynein depletion.
evidence: This interpretation is stated based on the experimental observations.

claim: Organization and orientation of the mitotic spindle requires attachment of cytoplasmic dynein to the cellular cortex in many organisms.
source: In many organisms, the organization and orientation of the mitotic spindle requires attachment of cytoplasmic dynein to the cellular cortex (Laan et al., 2012; Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Increasing concentrations of LatB gradually reduced the amount of F-actin in cultured Drosophila neurons.
source: We found that increasing concentrations of LatB gradually reduced the amount of F-actin, as judged by the intensity of rhodamine-phalloidin staining (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: In parallel with F-actin depolymerization, axons displayed an increased fraction of microtubules with plus-ends facing the cell body.
source: In parallel with F-actin depolymerization, axons displayed an increased fraction of microtubules with plus-ends facing the cell body (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At a high concentration of LatB (10 µM), when virtually no F-actin can be detected, about half of all EB1 comets moved toward the cell body in neurons.
source: At a high concentration of LatB (10 µM), when virtually no F-actin can be detected, about half of all EB1 comets moved toward the cell body, demonstrating that depolymerization of actin induced random microtubule orientation in neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Depolymerization of actin induced random microtubule orientation in neurons.
source: At a high concentration of LatB (10 µM), when virtually no F-actin can be detected, about half of all EB1 comets moved toward the cell body, demonstrating that depolymerization of actin induced random microtubule orientation in neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the LatB treatment data.

claim: Treatment with high LatB concentration induced accumulation of microtubule minus-ends at the tips of the axons in elav>GFP-CAMSAP3 neurons.
source: Treatment with high LatB concentration also induced accumulation of microtubule minus-ends at the tips of the axons in elav>GFP-CAMSAP3 neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Actin depolymerization phenocopied dynein depletion in axons.
source: These data show that actin depolymerization phenocopied dynein depletion in axons, suggesting that cortical dynein sorts microtubules.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the similarity of phenotypes between LatB treatment and dynein RNAi.

claim: LatB washout induced removal of GFP-CAMSAP3 from axon tips without affecting the length of the axon.
source: We observed that the LatB washout induced removal of GFP-CAMSAP3 from axon tips without affecting the length of the axon (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LatB washout did not result in the normal scattered distribution of minus-ends along the length of the axon observed in control neurons.
source: It should be mentioned that LatB washout did not result in the normal scattered distribution of minus-ends along the length of the axon observed in control neurons (Figure 2E, left panels).
evidence: This observation is stated with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: After LatB washout, minus-ends remained clustered in the shaft of the axon, most likely because by the time of drug washout these minus-end-out microtubules were already crosslinked into a bundle.
source: Instead, they remained clustered in the shaft, most likely because by the time of drug washout these minus-end-out microtubules were already crosslinked into a bundle.
evidence: This interpretation is stated to explain the observation.

claim: Treatment of S2 cells with high concentration of LatB induced formation of processes containing microtubules of mixed polarity.
source: As in the case of neurons, the treatment of S2 cells with high concentration of LatB induced formation of processes containing microtubules of mixed polarity (Figure 3C) and massive accumulation of minus-ends in their tips (Figure 3D–F; Video 9).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3C–F and Video 9.

claim: Treatment of S2 cells with high concentration of LatB induced massive accumulation of minus-ends in process tips.
source: As in the case of neurons, the treatment of S2 cells with high concentration of LatB induced formation of processes containing microtubules of mixed polarity (Figure 3C) and massive accumulation of minus-ends in their tips (Figure 3D–F; Video 9).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3C–F and Video 9.

claim: LatB washout in S2 cells resulted in robust movement of GFP-CAMSAP3 labeled minus-ends from the tips of processes toward the cell body.
source: Strikingly, LatB washout resulted in robust movement of GFP-CAMSAP3 labeled minus-ends from the tips of processes toward the cell body (Figure 3F, middle panel; Figure 3G; Video 9).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3F, 3G and Video 9.

claim: After dynein knockdown in S2 cells, LatB washout did not result in retrograde transport of microtubule minus-ends and the minus-ends caps stayed at the tips of processes.
source: However, if the same experiment was performed after dynein knockdown, retrograde transport of microtubule minus-ends was not observed and the minus-ends caps stay at the tips of processes (Figure 3F, right panel; Video 9), directly demonstrating the role of cortical dynein in removal of minus-end-out microtubules from processes to the cell body.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3F and Video 9.

claim: The LatB washout experiments directly demonstrate the role of cortical dynein in removal of minus-end-out microtubules from processes to the cell body.
source: However, if the same experiment was performed after dynein knockdown, retrograde transport of microtubule minus-ends was not observed and the minus-ends caps stay at the tips of processes (Figure 3F, right panel; Video 9), directly demonstrating the role of cortical dynein in removal of minus-end-out microtubules from processes to the cell body.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the LatB washout experiments.

claim: The FRB-FKBP dimerization system for dynein recruitment works in Drosophila S2 cells.
source: To confirm that the FRB-FKBP dimerization system for dynein recruitment works in Drosophila S2 cells, we first coexpressed a GFP construct fused to FRB (FRB-GFP) and the peroxisome membrane-targeting signal peptide coupled to the red fluorescent protein (PEX3-RFP-FKBP). In the absence of rapalog, the GFP signal appeared soluble in the cytoplasm. The addition of rapalog recruited FRB-GFP to peroxisomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental validation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of rapalog significantly increased the intensity of the GFP fluorescence at the plasma membrane due to recruitment of cytoplasmic BicD to the plasma membrane in S2 cells expressing FRB-GFP-BicD and GAP43-FKBP.
source: Quantification showed that addition of rapalog significantly increased the intensity of the GFP fluorescence due to recruitment of cytoplasmic BicD to the plasma membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on quantitative TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the absence of rapalog, CAMSAP3 accumulated in the processes of S2 cells treated with 10 µM LatB.
source: In the absence of rapalog, CAMSAP3 accumulated in the processes of S2 cells treated with 10 µM LatB.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: Before addition of rapalog, CAMSAP3 clusters marking positions of minus-ends were either static or pushing against the plasma membrane in S2 cells treated with LatB.
source: Time-lapse imaging before addition of the drug revealed that these CAMSAP3 clusters, marking positions of minus-ends, were either static or pushing against the plasma membrane (Video 10).
evidence: This is stated based on time-lapse imaging shown in Video 10.

claim: When the BicD-dynein complex was recruited to the membrane by addition of rapalog, CAMSAP3-labeled microtubule minus-ends robustly moved away from the tip toward the cell body in S2 cells treated with LatB.
source: However, when the BicD-dynein complex was recruited to the membrane by addition of rapalog, CAMSAP3-labeled microtubule minus-ends robustly moved away from the tip, toward the cell body (Figure 3H, top panels; Figure 3I; Video 10).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3H, 3I and Video 10.

claim: The same rapalog-induced BicD recruitment assay performed in DHC knockdown cells did not show removal of microtubule minus-ends.
source: The same assay performed in DHC knockdown cells did not show this removal of microtubule minus-ends (Figure 3H, bottom panels; Video 10).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3H and Video 10.

claim: Dynein is responsible for microtubule sorting, and this activity requires the attachment of the motor to the cortex mediated by actin filaments.
source: Taken together, these data confirmed that dynein is responsible for microtubule sorting, and this activity requires the attachment of the motor to the cortex mediated by actin filaments.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the LatB and dynein recruitment experiments.

claim: Mature axons contain microtubule arrays of uniform polarity with plus-ends facing away from the cell body (plus-end-out).
source: Mature axons contain microtubule arrays of uniform polarity with plus-ends facing away from the cell body (plus-end-out).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Discussion section.

claim: The axonal microtubule network undergoes dramatic reorganization during development.
source: Our data showed that the axonal microtubule network undergoes dramatic reorganization during development.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the time-course data presented in the study.

claim: At early stages of neurite formation, the minus-ends of sliding microtubules are pushed against the plasma membrane, generating the forces that drive initial neurite outgrowth.
source: At early stages of neurite formation, the minus-ends of sliding microtubules are pushed against the plasma membrane, generating the forces that drive initial neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on the experimental data.

claim: At early stages of neurite formation, growing neurites contain microtubule arrays of mixed orientation.
source: At this stage, growing neurites contain microtubule arrays of mixed orientation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on the experimental data.

claim: Later in development, axonal microtubule arrays are reorganized from mixed to uniform (plus-end-out) orientation.
source: However, later in development, axonal microtubule arrays are reorganized from mixed to uniform (plus-end-out) orientation, consistent with the well established microtubule organization described in mammalian (Baas et al., 1988) and Drosophila axons (Stone et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Cortical dynein drives the transition from mixed to uniform microtubule orientation by sliding and expelling minus-end-out microtubules from the axon toward the cell body.
source: Here, we demonstrated that cortical dynein drives this transition by sliding and expelling minus-end-out microtubules from the axon toward the cell body.
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion in the Discussion section based on the experimental data.

claim: Initial neurite formation in Drosophila neurons requires microtubule-microtubule sliding driven by kinesin-1.
source: We previously demonstrated that initial neurite formation in Drosophila neurons requires microtubule-microtubule sliding driven by kinesin-1.
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous work by the authors.

claim: Knockdown of kinesin-1 in primary neurons impairs the motility of interphase microtubules and causes neurons to fail to develop axons.
source: Knockdown of kinesin-1 in primary neurons impairs the motility of interphase microtubules and causes neurons to fail to develop axons (Lu et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Kinesin slides antiparallel microtubules against each other; if microtubules are oriented parallel to each other kinesin would bundle rather than slide them.
source: Furthermore, symmetry considerations dictate that kinesin slides antiparallel microtubules against each other; if microtubules are oriented parallel to each other kinesin would bundle rather than slide them (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of kinesin's properties and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Nascent growing neurites contain microtubule arrays with mixed polarity, which is required for microtubule sliding by kinesin-1.
source: First, nascent growing neurites contain microtubule arrays with mixed polarity. As mentioned above, this antiparallel orientation is required for microtubule sliding by kinesin-1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding that supports the kinesin-1 sliding model.

claim: Microtubule minus-ends are pushed against the plasma membrane at the tips of processes, generating the force for neurite outgrowth.
source: Second, microtubule minus-ends are pushed against the plasma membrane at the tips of processes, generating the force for neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated as a finding that supports the kinesin-1 sliding model.

claim: Mitotic kinesins such as kinesin-5 and kinesin-6 play an important role in the regulation of axon outgrowth.
source: Recent experimental data revealed that 'mitotic' kinesins, such as kinesin-5 (Nadar et al., 2008; Nadar et al., 2012) and kinesin-6 (Lin et al., 2012; del Castillo et al., 2015), play an important role in the regulation of axon outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: The well established function of mitotic motors is to reorganize and stabilize the mitotic spindle to facilitate chromosome segregation.
source: The well established function of these mitotic motors is to reorganize and stabilize the mitotic spindle to facilitate chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Mitotic motors accumulate in the spindle midzone where antiparallel microtubules coming from opposite poles overlap.
source: These motors accumulate in the spindle midzone where antiparallel microtubules coming from opposite poles overlap.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Developing Drosophila axons, like the spindle midzone, are filled with antiparallel microtubule arrays.
source: Our work shows that developing Drosophila axons, like the spindle midzone, are filled with antiparallel microtubule arrays.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current work.

claim: The same mechanisms controlling the mitotic spindle could be used to regulate axonal outgrowth.
source: This microtubule configuration suggests that the same mechanisms controlling the mitotic spindle could be used to regulate axonal outgrowth (Baas, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the similarity in microtubule organization.

claim: Mitotic kinesins control neurite outgrowth both in mammalian and Drosophila systems.
source: Interestingly, 'mitotic kinesins' control neurite outgrowth both in mammalian and Drosophila systems, which supports the idea that the molecular players that drive axon initiation and outgrowth in Drosophila may be conserved across species.
evidence: This is stated based on the literature and supports the conservation hypothesis.

claim: Minus-end-out microtubules are consistently observed at the early stages of neurite formation.
source: Our data show that minus-end-out microtubules are consistently observed at the early stages of neurite formation, while at later stages the vast majority of microtubules in axons have their plus-ends out, as have been reported in multiple published papers (Baas et al., 1988; Stepanova et al., 2003; Stone et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current work.

claim: At later stages the vast majority of microtubules in axons have their plus-ends out.
source: Our data show that minus-end-out microtubules are consistently observed at the early stages of neurite formation, while at later stages the vast majority of microtubules in axons have their plus-ends out, as have been reported in multiple published papers (Baas et al., 1988; Stepanova et al., 2003; Stone et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current work and supported by citations.

claim: Neurons must activate an additional sorting mechanism that eliminates 'wrong' polarity microtubules from axons.
source: Therefore, neurons must activate an additional sorting mechanism that eliminates these 'wrong' polarity microtubules from axons.
evidence: This is stated as a logical conclusion based on the observed transition in microtubule polarity.

claim: Dynein and dynein-associated proteins are required for correct microtubule orientation in axons of Drosophila da sensory neurons.
source: Previous studies reported that dynein and dynein-associated proteins are required for correct microtubule orientation in axons of Drosophila da sensory neurons (Zheng et al., 2008; Arthur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: Dynein knockdown caused mixed microtubule polarity in axons of cultured neurons.
source: Our results using cultured neurons are in full agreement with these studies, as dynein knockdown caused mixed microtubule polarity in axons.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current work that agrees with previous studies.

claim: Several studies have linked dynein-mediated microtubule reorganization to actin, both in interphase and in mitosis.
source: Interestingly, several studies have linked dynein-mediated microtubule reorganization to actin, both in interphase (Mazel et al., 2014) and in mitosis (Kotak et al., 2012; Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: Depolymerization of actin filaments (including cortical actin) using high concentrations of LatB causes the same defects in microtubule orientation as dynein knockdown.
source: In this study, we showed that depolymerization of actin filaments (including cortical actin) using high concentrations of LatB causes the same defects in microtubule orientation as dynein knockdown.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current work.

claim: Recovery of cortical actin after drug washout results in efficient dynein-driven removal of minus-end-out microtubules from the tips of processes.
source: Recovery of cortical actin after drug washout results in efficient dynein-driven removal of minus-end-out microtubules from the tips of processes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current work.

claim: The requirement for actin can be efficiently bypassed by direct recruitment of the dynein machinery directly to the plasma membrane.
source: Furthermore, the requirement for actin can be efficiently bypassed by direct recruitment of the dynein machinery directly to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current work.

claim: Microtubule sorting depends on the activity of cytoplasmic dynein attached to the cortical actin filament meshwork.
source: Therefore, we propose that microtubule sorting depends on the activity of cytoplasmic dynein attached to the cortical actin filament meshwork.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: Additional proteins that link actin and microtubule pathways in the neuron are likely involved in microtubule organization.
source: However, as we did not get complete recovery of the wild type distribution of microtubules in our LatB washout or dynein-membrane recruitment experiments, it is likely that additional proteins that link actin and microtubule pathways in the neuron are involved in microtubule organization; one good candidate is the well characterized actin-microtubule crosslinking protein Short stop (Lee and Kolodziej, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on incomplete recovery in experiments.

claim: Dynein activity is required for axon elongation.
source: In addition to the sorting activity described in this work, other groups have observed that dynein activity is required for axon elongation (Ahmad and Baas, 1995; Ahmad et al., 1998; Grabham et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: Dynein generates forces that push the cytoskeletal meshwork forward during axonal elongation in cultured chick sensory neurons.
source: A more recent study by Miller et al. has reported that dynein generates forces that push the cytoskeletal meshwork forward during axonal elongation in cultured chick sensory neurons (Roossien et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to published work.

claim: Cortical dynein can promote axon outgrowth after the initial stages of neurite outgrowth, when microtubules are sorted into a plus-end-out orientation.
source: In agreement with their data, we predict that cortical dynein can promote axon outgrowth after the initial stages of neurite outgrowth, when microtubules are sorted into a plus-end-out orientation.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the current findings and previous work.

claim: The direction of dynein-powered forces is dictated by the intrinsic orientation of microtubules.
source: Because the direction of dynein-powered forces is dictated by the intrinsic orientation of microtubules, microtubules with minus-end-out are redirected toward the cell body, whereas plus-end-out microtubules are transported toward the tip of the axon.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of dynein's motor properties.

claim: Dynein-driven microtubule transport can remove microtubules with the wrong orientation (minus-end-out) and also push microtubules of the right orientation (plus-end-out) toward the axon tip.
source: Therefore, dynein-driven microtubule transport can not only remove microtubules with the wrong orientation (minus-end-out) but also push microtubules of the right orientation (plus-end-out) toward the axon tip.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the understanding of dynein's activity.

claim: Dynein may play an important role in axonal microtubule maintenance.
source: In addition to the role of dynein in developing neurons, dynein may play an important role in axonal microtubule maintenance.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about dynein's role.

claim: Microtubule polymers require subunit turnover to maintain their integrity.
source: Microtubule polymers, like other protein structures, require subunit turnover to maintain their integrity.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about protein structures.

claim: Several microtubule severing proteins are able to fragment microtubules into short pieces.
source: It has been proposed that several microtubule severing proteins are able to fragment microtubules into short pieces (McNally and Vale, 1993).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to published work.

claim: Short microtubule seeds generated by severing may be reoriented by diffusion forces in either direction with equal probability.
source: In this scenario, short microtubule seeds are generated which may be reoriented by diffusion forces in either direction (plus-end-in or plus-end-out) with equal probability.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothetical scenario.

claim: Active bidirectional transport of short microtubule fragments in the axons has been described in cultured rat hippocampal neurons.
source: Indeed, active bidirectional transport of short microtubule fragments in the axons has been described in cultured rat hippocampal neurons (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to published work.

claim: The transport of short microtubule fragments in axons is driven by dynein.
source: The authors proposed that the transport of these short microtubule fragments is driven by dynein.
evidence: This is stated with reference to a published proposal.

claim: Microtubule fragments transported in the retrograde direction should be oriented with plus-ends toward the cell body while anterogradely transported fragments should have the opposite orientation.
source: Our prediction is that microtubule fragments transported in the retrograde direction should be oriented with plus-ends toward the cell body while anterogradely transported fragments should have the opposite orientation.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the authors' model.

claim: Kinesin-1 and dynein are the two major motors involved in reorganizing cytoplasmic microtubules in many different model systems.
source: It has been shown in many different model systems that kinesin-1 and dynein are the two major motors involved in reorganizing cytoplasmic microtubules (Fink and Steinberg, 2006; Straube et al., 2006; Jolly et al., 2010; Mazel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: Both kinesin-1 and dynein play an important role in axon formation.
source: Both motors play an important role in axon formation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the current work.

claim: The contribution of kinesin-1 and dynein differs at different developing stages of axon formation.
source: However, the contribution of each motor likely differs at different developing stages (see model described in Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to the model in Figure 4.

claim: In spherically shaped undifferentiated cells, kinesin-1 motors slide antiparallel microtubules perpendicularly to the plasma membrane with their minus-end-leading.
source: In spherically shaped undifferentiated cells, kinesin-1 motors slide antiparallel microtubules perpendicularly to the plasma membrane with their minus-end-leading (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as part of the model described in Figure 4A.

claim: Kinesin-1 sliding generates the force that breaks the symmetry of the cell and induces a deformation of the plasma membrane to initiate neurite outgrowth.
source: This sliding generates the force that breaks the symmetry of the cell and induces a deformation of the plasma membrane to initiate neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated as part of the model.

claim: During the initial stage of neurite formation, the role of cortical dynein is probably limited by steric restrictions.
source: During this stage, the role of cortical dynein is probably limited by steric restrictions.
evidence: This is stated as part of the model.

claim: Cortical dynein can only slide microtubules tangential to the plasma membrane, and therefore dynein-mediated movement cannot deform the membrane and initiate outgrowth.
source: Cortical dynein can only slide microtubules tangential to the plasma membrane, and therefore dynein-mediated movement cannot deform the membrane and initiate outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated as part of the model explaining why dynein doesn't contribute to initial outgrowth.

claim: Nascent neurites contain antiparallel microtubule arrays.
source: At the next stage, nascent neurites contain antiparallel microtubule arrays (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as part of the model described in Figure 4B.

claim: The antiparallel configuration in nascent neurites allows kinesin-1 to continue to drive antiparallel microtubule sliding.
source: This configuration allows kinesin-1 to continue to drive antiparallel microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is stated as part of the model.

claim: Once the processes start to form, the new geometry will allow cortical dynein to contribute to both microtubule organization and neurite outgrowth.
source: Once the processes start to form, the new geometry will allow cortical dynein to contribute to both microtubule organization and neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated as part of the model.

claim: Cortical dynein in the neurite cortex can only slide microtubules parallel to the axis of the process.
source: Cortical dynein in the neurite cortex can only slide microtubules parallel to the axis of the process.
evidence: This is stated as part of the model.

claim: The contribution of cortical dynein likely increases as the processes grow longer and thinner.
source: This contribution of cortical dynein likely increases as the processes grow longer (engaging more cortical dynein molecules) and thinner (allowing dynein to reach a larger fraction of microtubules in the processes).
evidence: This is stated as part of the model.

claim: Due to continuous dynein-powered sorting activity, the growing axon is mostly filled with uniformly oriented plus-end-out microtubules.
source: Due to continuous dynein-powered sorting activity, the growing axon is mostly filled with uniformly oriented plus-end-out microtubules.
evidence: This is stated as part of the model described in Figure 4C.

claim: At the stage when axons contain uniform microtubule arrays, dynein can continue removing minus-end-out microtubules and can contribute to axon elongation by pushing plus-end-out microtubules toward the tip.
source: At this stage, dynein can continue removing minus-end-out microtubules, and can contribute to axon elongation by pushing plus-end-out microtubules toward the tip (see Roossien et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as part of the model with reference to published work.

claim: At the stage when axons contain uniform microtubule arrays, kinesin-1 motors only bundle parallel microtubules and no longer contribute to microtubule sliding or outgrowth.
source: Note that at this stage, kinesin-1 motors only bundle parallel microtubules and no longer contribute to microtubule sliding or outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated as part of the model.

claim: Axons and dendrites are common morphologic features observed in neurons from ancestral metazoans to mammals.
source: Because axons and dendrites are common morphologic features observed in neurons from ancestral metazoans to mammals, we postulate that the same molecular mechanism presented here for axon formation in Drosophila neurons is conserved in other organisms.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about neuronal morphology.

claim: The same molecular mechanism presented for axon formation in Drosophila neurons is conserved in other organisms.
source: Because axons and dendrites are common morphologic features observed in neurons from ancestral metazoans to mammals, we postulate that the same molecular mechanism presented here for axon formation in Drosophila neurons is conserved in other organisms.
evidence: This is stated as a postulate based on the conservation of neuronal morphology.

claim: Microtubule orientation differs between axons and dendrites.
source: Microtubule orientation differs between axons and dendrites.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Axons are filled with uniformly oriented microtubules with plus-end-out.
source: While axons are filled with uniformly oriented microtubules with plus-end-out, dendrites contain either microtubules of mixed orientation (mammalian neurons) (Baas et al., 1988) or a majority of microtubules minus-end-out (Drosophila and C. elegans neurons) (Stone et al., 2008; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Dendrites in mammalian neurons contain microtubules of mixed orientation.
source: While axons are filled with uniformly oriented microtubules with plus-end-out, dendrites contain either microtubules of mixed orientation (mammalian neurons) (Baas et al., 1988) or a majority of microtubules minus-end-out (Drosophila and C. elegans neurons) (Stone et al., 2008; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Dendrites in Drosophila and C. elegans neurons contain a majority of microtubules minus-end-out.
source: While axons are filled with uniformly oriented microtubules with plus-end-out, dendrites contain either microtubules of mixed orientation (mammalian neurons) (Baas et al., 1988) or a majority of microtubules minus-end-out (Drosophila and C. elegans neurons) (Stone et al., 2008; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Neurons selectively employ cortical dynein to dictate which of the nascent neurites will become the future axon.
source: We speculate that neurons selectively employ cortical dynein to dictate which of the nascent neurites will become the future axon.
evidence: This is stated as speculation.

claim: The microtubule sliding activity or efficiency of dynein recruitment may be downregulated in dendrites.
source: It is likely that the microtubule sliding activity or efficiency of dynein recruitment may be downregulated in dendrites.
evidence: This is stated as speculation.

claim: Disruption of NudE, a dynein cofactor, impairs microtubule orientation in axons without affecting the orientation of dendritic microtubules in Drosophila da sensory neurons.
source: This hypothesis is in agreement with a recent study in Drosophila da sensory neurons showing that disruption of NudE, a dynein cofactor, impairs microtubule orientation in axons, without affecting the orientation of dendritic microtubules (Arthur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to published work.

claim: Kinesin-1 (unc-116) is required for minus-end-out orientation of microtubules in dendrites of C. elegans neurons.
source: Furthermore, Yan et al. directly demonstrated that kinesin-1 (unc-116) is required for minus-end-out orientation of microtubules in dendrites (Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to published work.

claim: The activity of cortical dynein is downregulated in dendrites, thus preserving the initial minus-end-out orientation of microtubules created by kinesin.
source: Those observations support the idea that the activity of cortical dynein is downregulated in dendrites, thus preserving the initial minus-end-out orientation of microtubules created by kinesin.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the cited observations.
